  a.distance(b), a.hausdorff_distance(b)

  geom.buffer(distance)           # expand/shrink geometry

Useful helpers:

# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.

# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. ```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_processing.rst

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

# Get violating spaces from ground truth
violating_guids = ['10mjSDZJj9gPS2PrQaxa3z', '10mjSDZJj9gPS2PrQaxa4o']

# Find these spaces and examine their geometry
for guid in violating_guids:
    space = model.by_guid(guid)
    print(f"\nSpace GUID: {guid}")
    print(f"  Name: {space.Name}")
    print(f"  LongName: {space.LongName}")
    
    # Extract geometry
    settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
    settings.set(settings.USE_WORLD_COORDS, True)
    try:
        shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, space)
        
        # Get vertices and faces
        verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
        faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)
        
        # Create trimesh
        mesh = trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=verts, faces=faces)
        
        print(f"  Bounds: {mesh.bounds}")
        print(f"  Extents: {mesh.extents}")
        
        # Get horizontal section at mid-height
        min_z, max_z = mesh.bounds[:, 2]
        mid_z = (min_z + max_z) / 2
        
        section = mesh.section(plane_origin=[0, 0, mid_z], plane_normal=[0, 0, 1])
        if section:
            path2d = section.to_planar()[0]
            polygons = path2d.polygons_full
            if polygons:
                poly = polygons[0]
                print(f"  2D Polygon area: {poly.area}")
                print(f"  Polygon bounds: {poly.bounds}")
                
                # Calculate maximum inscribed circle diameter
                # This is complex, so let's use a simpler approximation first
                min_rect = poly.minimum_rotated_rectangle
                width, height = min_rect.bounds[2] - min_rect.bounds[0], min_rect.bounds[3] - min_rect.bounds[1]
                print(f"  Mins bounding rect: {width} x {height}")
                min_dim = min(width, height)
                print(f"  Min dimension (approx diameter): {min_dim}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  Error extracting geometry: {e}")

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_processing.rst

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]

    geometry = shape.geometry # see #1124
    # These are methods of the TopoDS_Shape class from pythonOCC

    # These are methods of the gpXYZ class from pythonOCC

except:

import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import trimesh
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Polygon
from typing import List, Dict, Any
import math

def get_minimum_width(polygon: Polygon, num_angles: int = 36) -> float:
    """Calculate the minimum width of a polygon by rotating and checking bounding box.
    
    This approximates the maximum diameter of a circle that can fit inside the polygon.
    """
    min_width = float('inf')
    
    for i in range(num_angles):
        angle_deg = i * (180.0 / num_angles)
        angle_rad = math.radians(angle_deg)
        
        # Rotate polygon
        rotated = shapely.affinity.rotate(polygon, angle_deg, origin='centroid')
        
        # Get bounding box
        minx, miny, maxx, maxy = rotated.bounds
        width = maxx - minx
        height = maxy - miny
        
        # Minimum dimension is the limiting factor for a circle
        min_dim = min(width, height)
        min_width = min(min_width, min_dim)

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]

# Function to calculate max inscribed circle diameter from polygon
def get_max_diameter(poly):
    """Calculate the maximum inscribed circle diameter from a polygon."""
    # Method 1: Use minimum rotated rectangle
    min_rect = poly.minimum_rotated_rectangle
    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = min_rect.bounds
    # The minimum dimension of the bounding box gives us the max circle diameter
    return min(maxx - minx, maxy - miny)

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]

# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]

This snippet demonstrates how to add various subcontexts to an IFC model using the IFCopenShell API. These contexts define different geometric purposes such as 'Body', 'Axis', 'Box', and 'Annotation' for 3D, plan, section, and elevation views. It requires the 'ifcopenshell.api.context' module.

```python
import ifcopenshell.api.context

# Assuming 'model', 'model3d', and 'plan' are pre-defined IFC objects

# Add 'Body' context for 3D model view
body = ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Body", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 3D graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 2D plan graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Box' context for 3D model view (useful for clash detection)

    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Box", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D plan view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="PLAN_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D section view

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_processing.rst

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_creation.rst

This snippet demonstrates how to add various subcontexts to an IFC model using the IFCopenShell API. These contexts define different geometric purposes such as 'Body', 'Axis', 'Box', and 'Annotation' for 3D, plan, section, and elevation views. It requires the 'ifcopenshell.api.context' module.

```python
import ifcopenshell.api.context

# Assuming 'model', 'model3d', and 'plan' are pre-defined IFC objects

# Add 'Body' context for 3D model view
body = ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Body", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 3D graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 2D plan graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Box' context for 3D model view (useful for clash detection)
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Box", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D plan view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="PLAN_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D section view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="SECTION_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D elevation view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,

### Process IFC Element to Shape Data (Python)

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_processing.rst

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

        >>> print(f"Found {len(violating_guids)} violations")
    """

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".

import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Polygon, MultiPolygon
import trimesh

def get_max_diameter(poly):
    """Calculate the maximum inscribed circle diameter from a polygon."""
    min_rect = poly.minimum_rotated_rectangle
    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = min_rect.bounds
    return min(maxx - minx, maxy - miny)

def check_model(path):
    """Test the checking algorithm on a model."""
    model = ifcopenshell.open(path)
    
    # Get all spaces and prepare for classification
    spaces_data = []
    for space in model.by_type('IfcSpace'):
        spaces_data.append({
            'guid': space.GlobalId,
            'name': space.LongName or space.Name or ''
        })
    
    # Classify spaces
    classified = classify_spaces(spaces_data, path)
    
    # Define applicable classifications
    applicable = {'Balcony', 'Circulation', 'Garage', 'Habitable', 'Institutional', 
                  'Lobby', 'Mercantile', 'Office', 'Parking', 'Production', 
                  'Refuge', 'Stair Hall', 'Workplace'}
    
    settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
    violations = []
    skipped = 0
    
    for space_info in classified:
        classification = space_info.get('classification', 'Unclassified')
        if classification not in applicable:
            continue
        
        space = model.by_guid(space_info['guid'])
        
        try:
            shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, space)
            grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
            grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)
            
            mesh = trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=grouped_verts, faces=grouped_faces)
            
            # Take cross-section at mid-height
            z_level = mesh.bounds[0, 2] + (mesh.extents[2] / 2)
            
            section = mesh.section(plane_origin=[0, 0, z_level], plane_normal=[0, 0, 1])
            
            if section:
                path2d = section.to_planar()[0]
                
                if hasattr(path2d, 'polygons_full') and len(path2d.polygons_full) > 0:
                    poly = path2d.polygons_full[0]
                    max_diameter = get_max_diameter(poly)
                    
                    if max_diameter < 1.52:
                        violations.append(space_info['guid'])
                else:
                    skipped += 1
            else:
                skipped += 1
                
        except Exception as e:
            skipped += 1
    
    if skipped > 0:
        print(f"  Warning: Skipped {skipped} spaces")
    return violations

# Test on all models
models = [
    ('/home/sffc348/Repos/cobbie/acc/bim_models/141/arc.ifc', []),

]

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_processing.rst

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]

### Add IFC Subcontexts using IFCopenShell API

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_creation.rst

This snippet demonstrates how to add various subcontexts to an IFC model using the IFCopenShell API. These contexts define different geometric purposes such as 'Body', 'Axis', 'Box', and 'Annotation' for 3D, plan, section, and elevation views. It requires the 'ifcopenshell.api.context' module.

```python
import ifcopenshell.api.context

# Assuming 'model', 'model3d', and 'plan' are pre-defined IFC objects

# Add 'Body' context for 3D model view
body = ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Body", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 3D graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 2D plan graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Box' context for 3D model view (useful for clash detection)
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Box", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D plan view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="PLAN_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D section view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="SECTION_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D elevation view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="ELEVATION_VIEW", parent=plan)

import ifcopenshell

shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)

### Add IFC Subcontexts using IFCopenShell API

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_creation.rst

This snippet demonstrates how to add various subcontexts to an IFC model using the IFCopenShell API. These contexts define different geometric purposes such as 'Body', 'Axis', 'Box', and 'Annotation' for 3D, plan, section, and elevation views. It requires the 'ifcopenshell.api.context' module.

```python
import ifcopenshell.api.context

# Assuming 'model', 'model3d', and 'plan' are pre-defined IFC objects

# Add 'Body' context for 3D model view
body = ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Body", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 3D graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 2D plan graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Box' context for 3D model view (useful for clash detection)
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Box", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D plan view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="PLAN_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D section view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="SECTION_VIEW", parent=plan)

# Add 'Annotation' context for 2D elevation view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Annotation", target_view="ELEVATION_VIEW", parent=plan)
```

import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:

    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_creation.rst

This snippet demonstrates how to add various subcontexts to an IFC model using the IFCopenShell API. These contexts define different geometric purposes such as 'Body', 'Axis', 'Box', and 'Annotation' for 3D, plan, section, and elevation views. It requires the 'ifcopenshell.api.context' module.

```python
import ifcopenshell.api.context

# Assuming 'model', 'model3d', and 'plan' are pre-defined IFC objects

# Add 'Body' context for 3D model view
body = ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Body", target_view="MODEL_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 3D graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Model", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=model3d)

# Add 'Axis' context for 2D plan graph view
ifcopenshell.api.context.add_context(model,
    context_type="Plan", context_identifier="Axis", target_view="GRAPH_VIEW", parent=plan)

def check_304_3_1_circular_space(path_ifc_model: str) -> List[str]:
    """
    Check if spaces have enough room for wheelchair turning space with minimum diameter of 1.52m.
    
    Rule 304.3.1 Circular Space: Circular space shall have a diameter of 1.52 m (60 inches) minimum.
    
    Applicable Space Classifications: Balcony, Circulation, Garage, Habitable, Institutional,
    Lobby, Mercantile, Office, Parking, Production, Refuge, Stair Hall, Workplace.
    
    Args:
        path_ifc_model: Path to the IFC model file.
        
    Returns:
        List of IFC GUIDs of spaces that violate the rule (diameter < 1.52m).
        
    Example:
        >>> violations = check_304_3_1_circular_space('/path/to/model.ifc')
        >>> print(f"Found {len(violations)} violations")
    """
    # Load model
    model = ifcopenshell.open(path_ifc_model)
    
    # Get all spaces
    spaces = model.by_type('IfcSpace')
    if not spaces:
        return []
    
    # Prepare spaces for classification
    spaces_data = [{"guid": s.GlobalId, "name": s.LongName or s.Name or ""} for s in spaces]
    
    # Classify spaces

    # Create lookup dictionary for classifications

    # Applicable classifications
    applicable_classifications = {
        'Balcony', 'Circulation', 'Garage', 'Habitable', 'Institutional',
        'Lobby', 'Mercantile', 'Office', 'Parking', 'Production',
        'Refuge', 'Stair Hall', 'Workplace'
    }
    
    # Minimum required diameter (1.52 m)
    min_required_diameter = 1.52
    
    violating_guids = []
    skipped = 0
    
    # Geometry settings
    settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
    settings.set(settings.USE_WORLD_COORDS, True)
    
    for space in spaces:
        guid = space.GlobalId
        
        # Skip spaces not in applicable classifications
        classification = classification_map.get(guid, 'Unclassified')
        if classification not in applicable_classifications:
            continue
        
        try:
            # Extract geometry
            shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, space)
            verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
            faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)
            
            # Create trimesh
            mesh = trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=verts, faces=faces)
            
            # Get bounds to determine mid-height for horizontal section
            min_z, max_z = mesh.bounds[:, 2]
            
            # Skip if space has no height
            if max_z - min_z < 0.01:

            mid_z = (min_z + max_z) / 2
            
            # Get horizontal section
            section = mesh.section(plane_origin=[0, 0, mid_z], plane_normal=[0, 0, 1])
            
            if section is None:

            # Calculate minimum bounding rectangle dimensions

            minx, miny, maxx, maxy = min_rect.bounds
            width = maxx - minx
            height = maxy - miny

import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape
import numpy as np
import trimesh
import shapely.geometry
from typing import List


def check_304_3_1_circular_space(path_ifc_model: str) -> List[str]:
    """
    Check if spaces have enough room for wheelchair turning space with minimum diameter of 1.52m.
    
    Rule 304.3.1 Circular Space: Circular space shall have a diameter of 1.52 m (60 inches) minimum.
    
    Applicable Space Classifications: Balcony, Circulation, Garage, Habitable, Institutional,
    Lobby, Mercantile, Office, Parking, Production, Refuge, Stair Hall, Workplace.
    
    Args:
        path_ifc_model: Path to the IFC model file.
        
    Returns:
        List of IFC GUIDs of spaces that violate the rule (diameter < 1.52m).
        
    Example:
        >>> violations = check_304_3_1_circular_space('/path/to/model.ifc')
        >>> print(f"Found {len(violations)} violations")
    """
    # Load model
    model = ifcopenshell.open(path_ifc_model)
    
    # Get all spaces
    spaces = model.by_type('IfcSpace')
    if not spaces:
        return []
    
    # Prepare spaces for classification
    spaces_data = [{"guid": s.GlobalId, "name": s.LongName or s.Name or ""} for s in spaces]
    
    # Classify spaces
    classified_spaces = classify_spaces(spaces_data, path_ifc_model)
    
    # Create lookup dictionary for classifications
    classification_map = {s['guid']: s['classification'] for s in classified_spaces}
    
    # Applicable classifications
    applicable_classifications = {
        'Balcony', 'Circulation', 'Garage', 'Habitable', 'Institutional',
        'Lobby', 'Mercantile', 'Office', 'Parking', 'Production',
        'Refuge', 'Stair Hall', 'Workplace'
    }
    
    # Minimum required diameter (1.52 m)
    min_required_diameter = 1.52
    
    violating_guids = []
    skipped = 0
    
    # Geometry settings
    settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
    settings.set(settings.USE_WORLD_COORDS, True)
    
    for space in spaces:
        guid = space.GlobalId
        
        # Skip spaces not in applicable classifications
        classification = classification_map.get(guid, 'Unclassified')
        if classification not in applicable_classifications:
            continue
        
        try:
            # Extract geometry
            shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, space)
            verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
            faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)
            
            # Create trimesh
            mesh = trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=verts, faces=faces)
            
            # Get bounds to determine mid-height for horizontal section
            min_z, max_z = mesh.bounds[:, 2]
            
            # Skip if space has no height
            if max_z - min_z < 0.01:
                skipped += 1
                continue
            
            mid_z = (min_z + max_z) / 2
            
            # Get horizontal section
            section = mesh.section(plane_origin=[0, 0, mid_z], plane_normal=[0, 0, 1])
            
            if section is None:
                skipped += 1
                continue
            
            # Convert to 2D planar path
            path2d = section.to_planar()[0]
            polygons = path2d.polygons_full
            
            if not polygons:
                skipped += 1
                continue
            
            # Use the first polygon (main floor area)
            poly = polygons[0]
            
            # Calculate minimum bounding rectangle dimensions
            min_rect = poly.minimum_rotated_rectangle
            minx, miny, maxx, maxy = min_rect.bounds
            width = maxx - minx
            height = maxy - miny
            
            # Use the minimum dimension as an approximation of the largest possible diameter
            # This is a conservative estimate - the actual largest inscribed circle may be larger
            max_diameter = min(width, height)
            
            # Check violation
            if max_diameter < min_required_diameter:
                violating_guids.append(guid)
                
        except (AttributeError, RuntimeError, ValueError) as e:
            skipped += 1
            continue
    
    if skipped > 0:
        print(f"Warning: Skipped {skipped} spaces due to geometry processing issues")
    
    return violating_guids


# Test the function on all models

]

for model_path in test_models:

        print(f"  Violations: {len(violations)}")

def get_minimum_width(polygon: Polygon, num_angles: int = 36) -> float:
    """Calculate the minimum width of a polygon by rotating and checking bounding box.
    
    This approximates the maximum diameter of a circle that can fit inside the polygon.
    """
    min_width = float('inf')
    
    for i in range(num_angles):
        angle_deg = i * (180.0 / num_angles)
        angle_rad = math.radians(angle_deg)
        
        # Rotate polygon
        rotated = shapely.affinity.rotate(polygon, angle_deg, origin='centroid')
        
        # Get bounding box
        minx, miny, maxx, maxy = rotated.bounds
        width = maxx - minx
        height = maxy - miny
        
        # Minimum dimension is the limiting factor for a circle
        min_dim = min(width, height)
        min_width = min(min_width, min_dim)
    
    return min_width

import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

Source: https://github.com/ifcopenshell/ifcopenshell/blob/v0.8.0/src/ifcopenshell-python/docs/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_processing.rst

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

This Python snippet demonstrates how to open an IFC file, select an IfcWall element, and process it into a shape using ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(). It shows how to extract the element's GUID, ID, geometry ID, transformation matrix, vertices, edges, faces, and material information. This is useful for understanding individual geometry processing but not recommended for practical applications due to performance limitations.

```python
import ifcopenshell
import ifcopenshell.geom
import ifcopenshell.util.shape

ifc_file = ifcopenshell.open('model.ifc')
element = ifc_file.by_type('IfcWall')[0]

settings = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

# The GUID of the element we processed
print(shape.guid)

# The ID of the element we processed
print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
print(ifc_file.by_guid(shape.guid))

# A unique geometry ID, useful to check whether or not two geometries are
# identical for caching and reuse. The naming scheme is:
# IfcShapeRepresentation.id{-layerset-LayerSet.id}{-material-Material.id}{-openings-[Opening n.id ...]}{-world-coords}
print(shape.geometry.id)

# A 4x4 matrix representing the location and rotation of the element, in the form:
# [ [ x_x, y_x, z_x, x   ]
#   [ x_y, y_y, z_y, y   ]
#   [ x_z, y_z, z_z, z   ]
#   [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 ] ]
# The position is given by the last column: (x, y, z)
# The rotation is described by the first three columns, by explicitly specifying the local X, Y, Z axes.
# The first column is a normalised vector of the local X axis: (x_x, x_y, x_z)
# The second column is a normalised vector of the local Y axis: (y_x, y_y, y_z)
# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)
# The axes follow a right-handed coordinate system.
# Objects are never scaled, so the scale factor of the matrix is always 1.
matrix = shape.transformation.matrix

# For convenience, you might want the matrix as a nested numpy array, so you can do matrix math.
matrix = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_shape_matrix(shape)

# You can also extract the XYZ location of the matrix.
location = matrix[:,3][0:3]

# X Y Z of vertices in flattened list e.g. [v1x, v1y, v1z, v2x, v2y, v2z, ...]
# These vertices are local relative to the shape's transformation matrix.
verts = shape.geometry.verts

# Indices of vertices per edge e.g. [e1v1, e1v2, e2v1, e2v2, ...]
# If the geometry is mesh-like, edges contain the original edges.
# These may be quads or ngons and not necessarily triangles.
edges = shape.geometry.edges

# Indices of vertices per triangle face e.g. [f1v1, f1v2, f1v3, f2v1, f2v2, f2v3, ...]
# Note that faces are always triangles.
faces = shape.geometry.faces

# Since the lists are flattened, you may prefer to group them like so depending on your geometry kernel
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[v1x, v1y, v1z], [v2x, v2y, v2z], ...]
grouped_verts = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_vertices(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[e1v1, e1v2], [e2v1, e2v2], ...]
grouped_edges = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_edges(shape.geometry)
# A nested numpy array e.g. [[f1v1, f1v2, f1v3], [f2v1, f2v2, f2v3], ...]
grouped_faces = ifcopenshell.util.shape.get_faces(shape.geometry)

# A list of styles that are relevant to this shape
styles = shape.geometry.materials

for style in styles:
    # Each style is named after the entity class if a default
    # material is applied. Otherwise, it is named "surface-style-{SurfaceStyle.name}"
    # All non-alphanumeric characters are replaced with a "-".
    print(style.original_name())

    # A more human readable name
    print(style.name)

    # Each style may have diffuse colour RGB codes
    if style.has_diffuse:
        print(style.diffuse)

    # Each style may have transparency data
    if style.has_transparency:
        print(style.transparency)

# Indices of material applied per triangle face e.g. [f1m, f2m, ...]
material_ids = shape.geometry.material_ids

# IDs representation item per triangle face e.g. [f1i, f2i, ...]
item_ids = shape.geometry.item_ids

# The third column is a normalised vector of the local Z axis: (z_x, z_y, z_z)

shape = ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(settings, element)

print(shape.id)

# The element we are processing
